messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos had always taken pride in his work as a maid at the upscale hotel downtown. It was a far cry from the streets of Honduras he grew up on, where the constant sound of gunfire and screams still echoed in his mind. He tried not to think about it, but certain things triggered memories - like seeing cars that looked similar to the one he was stuffed into when the soldiers took him away. On those days, Carlos would try to avoid talking to anyone at work, fearing they might ask him what was wrong and inadvertently remind him of the event. One day, while cleaning a room, Carlos saw an episode of a TV show on the guest's laptop that depicted torture scenes eerily similar to his own experience. He immediately felt his heart racing, palms sweating, and had to take a break outside for some air. When he returned, he couldn't shake off the feeling of unease, constantly checking over his shoulder, as if expecting someone to jump out at him. Carlos was particularly jumpy when it came to strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations like ordering food or asking for directions. At night, Carlos would lie awake, listening intently for any sounds that might indicate an intruder - creaks of the floorboards, rustling outside his window. If someone touched him unexpectedly, he'd flinch and spin around, ready to defend himself. He smoked more than ever before, trying to calm his nerves, but it only seemed to make things worse. It was on one such sleepless night that Carlos had a panic attack, thinking the hotel's security guard had followed him home. The uniformed man seemed menacing in the dark alleyway outside Carlos' apartment, and he sprinted back inside, locking all doors and windows before collapsing onto his bed. This incident reinforced Carlos' decision to avoid authority figures whenever possible - no more going to the bank or attending public gatherings if it meant being around police officers or security personnel. As days went by, Carlos found himself increasingly withdrawn from friends and family, avoiding any conversations that might lead them to ask about his past. He started to skip social events or turn down invitations from coworkers, choosing instead to stay home alone with a cigarette and the TV blaring in the background - anything to distract him from the constant threat he felt lurking around every corner. The anxiety was taking its toll on Carlos' work performance too. Guests began complaining about his distant demeanor and lack of attention to detail when cleaning their rooms. His manager called him aside one day, concerned that something was wrong. But Carlos just shrugged it off, muttering something about needing a raise or being overworked. Carlos knew things couldn't go on like this forever, but he didn't know what else to do. He started having trouble sleeping again, waking up drenched in sweat after nightmares of the torture chamber. One morning, after an especially rough night, Carlos realized he needed help - he couldn't keep running from his memories and emotions any longer. With great trepidation, Carlos scheduled an appointment with a therapist specializing in trauma cases, hoping that finally talking about what happened might be the first step towards healing.
